name: Tomas Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the assistant manager at Hollow Oak Orchards, sixty hectares of apples and pears on the slope above the river. Right now it's pruning season, so I'm out with the crew from eight, and in the evenings I'm on the laptop going through the frost alerts and the spray plan. Last autumn we trialled a picking robot with little suction arms, and I basically adopted it. My partner Ines, she's a nurse, says I talk to it more than to her.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it to check spray timings against the weather, I use an app that counts fruitlets from photos, and I wrote half of our grant bid for the new hail nets with it. It's wrong sometimes, so I check, but it saves me hours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hail and the bank, in that order. One storm in July can knock thirty percent off the crop. And the margins on pears are so thin that one bad year and the owners start talking about pulling trees out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, just not magic. I'd tell the other growers at the fruit group it's worth using for the boring bits, records, spray plans, grant forms. Online I'd probably post a few tips, I do that already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down. I like the stuff, and I was hoping the picking robots would get good enough to fix our labour problem, because finding pickers gets harder every year. If it stalls, we're back to begging agencies for crews in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what works and stop paying for the tools that don't. I'd put some of my savings into the cider side business I've been planning with Ines's brother, because that doesn't depend on any of this. And I'd keep pushing the owners to join the regional growers' co-op so we can share machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a new variety that tastes fine but nothing special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Isn't a plateau safer for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, yes, probably. But I'm twenty-seven, and I'd like the work to get less backbreaking for the pickers. I'm not scared of change, I'm scared of standing still while the costs go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the cider plan.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's brother Teo has an old barn and a press. We'd use the fruit that the supermarkets reject for size, which is a crime to waste. I've put about four thousand into it already.

S0.say: He'd say AI is still a good tool, just not magic, worth using for records, spray plans and grant forms. He'd share tips with other growers at the fruit group and online.
S0.think: He'd be privately let down, because he hoped picking robots would solve the orchard's growing labour shortage. A plateau sends them back to begging agencies for pickers every September.
S0.do: Keeps the tools that work and cancels the rest, puts more savings into a cider side business with his partner's brother, and keeps pushing the owners to join the regional growers' co-op to share machines.
S0.feel: Calm but a little flat and disappointed.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of change, I'm scared of standing still while the costs go up.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is the rare farmer who hears the plateau as mild bad news. His worry is labour and costs, not machines, and he already treats AI as an everyday tool. He's quietly building a side income from waste fruit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now this is the one I kind of expect, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if we share it out properly. Robots for the heavy picking, people for the skilled pruning and the decisions, and proper training paid for by the industry. I'd say it on the growers' forum and probably write something for the co-op newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of it. I already know the robot, I know the software, and the owners trust me with it. What I worry about is the pickers, and the growers who can't afford the machines and get bought out by big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners to make me the person in charge of the robot fleet, and I'd want a pay rise for it, in writing. I'd push hard for the co-op to buy robots together so small orchards aren't wiped out. And I'd run a free evening class for the pickers who want to become operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. With a knot of worry about the small growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said big companies might buy out small growers. Who would you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robots. The rules. If only the big players can get the loans and the subsidies, of course they win. That's a political choice, and it can be made differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a picker who's been coming to Hollow Oak for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come and learn the machine with me, I'll show you. There's a lad, Dario, who's been here five seasons and he's sharper than half the managers I know. I'd want him running a robot, not on a plane home.

S1.say: He'd say it's good news if shared properly: robots for heavy picking, people for skilled pruning and decisions, and training paid for by the industry. He'd say it on the growers' forum and in the co-op newsletter.
S1.think: He expects to do well out of it, since he already knows the robot and the software. His worry is for pickers and for small growers who can't afford machines and get bought out.
S1.do: Asks to be put in charge of the robot fleet with a written pay rise, pushes the co-op to buy robots together, and runs a free evening class for pickers who want to become operators.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a knot of worry for the small growers.
S1.quote: Not the robots. The rules. If only the big players can get the loans and the subsidies, of course they win.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas sees steady disruption as a promotion for himself and a political fight for everyone else. He blames rules and loan access, not technology, which fits his progressive outlook. He'd use his head start to bring pickers like Dario with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. OK. That's the robot on steroids, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle fairly, and the government needs to step in with real money, like a basic income, straight away. I'd still say the technology itself isn't evil. It's who owns it and what they do with the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even my job goes. Two years ago I was the guy who knew the robot. In 2028 the robot knows itself. I'd be very good at a job nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd put a chunk of my savings into the cider business, because a small brand with a story might still sell when everything else is made by machines. I'd try to get the orchard owners to let the co-op buy shares in the robots rather than rent them. And I'd keep using every AI tool I can, to run the cider side with almost no staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Strange, because I like this stuff, but two years is a car crash, not a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't plan a career, I can only grab things. Grab the cider, grab a share of the robots, grab some land if it's cheap. It's survival mode, not strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run the cider business with almost no staff. Doesn't that clash with what you said about sharing the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does, you got me. I'd tell myself it's different because it's small and it's ours. I'm not sure that's true.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle fairly and call for government money such as a basic income straight away. He'd still argue the technology isn't evil; ownership and use of the savings are the problem.
S2.think: He thinks even his own job goes: his edge was knowing the robot, and by 2028 the robot runs itself. He'd be very good at a job nobody needs.
S2.do: Puts a chunk of savings into the cider business at once, pushes the owners to let the co-op buy shares in the robots instead of renting them, and uses AI to run the cider side with almost no staff.
S2.feel: Anxious, which surprises him given how much he likes the technology.
S2.quote: In 2028 the robot knows itself. I'd be very good at a job nobody needs.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most AI-friendly persona in this group finds two years too fast to plan; he calls it survival mode, not strategy. When challenged, he admitted the clash between sharing gains and running his own business with no staff. That honesty was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit more breathing room. Still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to make sure the orchards don't all end up owned by two companies. I'd be on every committee going, pushing for co-op ownership of the machines and public money for it. Same message as before, just louder and with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is enough for me to switch from being an orchard worker to being a part-owner of something. If I can't own the robots, I want to own a bit of the business that uses them. Otherwise I'm just watching from the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd grow the cider business properly, get it into some local shops and pubs. By year two I'd try to buy into Hollow Oak itself, even just ten percent, using my savings and maybe a loan against the cider. And I'd be the one testing every new robot on the farm, so I know what's coming before the owners do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but energised. Like the week before harvest when you've got a plan and you're just hoping the weather holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ines agree to putting savings into the farm and a loan on the cider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want to see the numbers twice and she'd make me promise not to touch the money we've set aside for a flat. That's fair. She's the steady one, I'm the one with ideas at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years that you wouldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd grab. With five I'd build, the cider, a stake in the orchard, a seat on the co-op board. Five years is enough time to own something instead of just being in the way of it.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years to stop the orchards ending up owned by two companies, and he'd push every committee for co-op ownership of the machines and public money to pay for it.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to move from worker to part-owner. If he can't own the robots, he wants to own part of a business that uses them, rather than watch from outside.
S3.do: Grows the cider business into local shops and pubs in year one, tries to buy about ten percent of the orchard by year two with savings and a loan, and tests every new robot on the farm first.
S3.feel: Anxious but energised, like the week before harvest with a plan in hand.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to own something instead of just being in the way of it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Tomas switches from grabbing to building, and ownership becomes his main idea of safety. His partner Ines acts as a brake and protects their flat savings. His politics and his plans line up more neatly here than in the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway. I could do a lot with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case for getting it right. Ten years to change the rules on ownership, set up co-ops, retrain people. If we mess it up with ten years' notice, that's on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine and maybe more than fine. I'd have time to build the cider brand, own part of the orchard and maybe learn something completely new on top. The risk is that I'd get comfortable and think I'm clever, and miss the bit where it all speeds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd write a ten-year plan with Ines, with money for the flat, money for the cider and money for a part-time course in something like agricultural engineering. I'd keep testing every robot. And I'd put real time into the co-op, because in ten years who owns what matters more than who knows what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. There's a worry under it, but it's a quiet one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is getting comfortable. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me in 2033, with a nice cider label, telling everyone it's fine, while the big growers quietly buy up every orchard in the valley. I've seen that happen with dairy farms round here. Nobody noticed until it was done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want young people starting in orchards now to hear from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the trees and learn the machines, both. And get your name on something, a co-op share, a bit of land, anything. Skills go out of date, ownership doesn't.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is the best chance of getting it right: time to change the ownership rules, set up co-ops and retrain people. If it goes wrong with that much warning, it's on all of us.
S4.think: He expects to do well, building the cider brand, owning part of the orchard and learning something new. His private risk is getting comfortable and missing the moment it speeds up.
S4.do: Writes a ten-year plan with his partner in the first year that splits money between a flat, the cider business and a part-time agricultural engineering course. Keeps testing robots and puts real time into the co-op.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and a little excited, with a quiet worry underneath.
S4.quote: Skills go out of date, ownership doesn't.
S4.fieldNote: Tomas is at his most confident with ten years and his main fear is his own complacency. The dairy buy-outs he has watched in the valley shape that fear. Across all three AGI pictures, his answer is ownership, and only the speed changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I like the technology and even I can't keep up with two years. What would help is public money for workers and co-ops to buy into the machines, not just grants for big farms to replace people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets to decide which robot comes to the farm. Right now it's the owner and the salesman. I'd want the people who actually work the trees in that room.

headlineQuote: In 2028 the robot knows itself. I'd be very good at a job nobody needs.
portrait: Tomas Wagner is a 27-year-old assistant manager on an apple and pear orchard who uses AI every day and has already trialled a picking robot. He's keen on the technology and progressive in his politics, so he blames rules and ownership, not machines, for what could go wrong. In the slow pictures he expects to come out ahead and tries to bring pickers with him. In the fast one he admits even his skills become useless, and he switches to grabbing assets like his cider business and a stake in the orchard. With more time his answer is always the same: own something, ideally together with other workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even someone who likes the technology couldn't keep up with two years.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for workers and co-ops to buy into the machines, instead of grants that only help big farms replace people.
